entries.answer: That's five questions in one, so let me take it in pieces. Winning aspiration — being the system small home-care agencies choose over CareLineLive without ever having to go up against the big enterprise players. Where we play — agencies running somewhere between forty and, say, a hundred and fifty carers, that's roughly our current book. How we win — compliance that actually holds up in a CQC inspection, that's the thing they tell me they bought us for. Capabilities and management systems I'm less sharp on, that's more Ellie's end of the conversation than mine.

We think about this a lot, honestly — Ellie and I go back and forth on strategy most weeks. Our whole approach is built around agencies feeling like the software understands their world, not some generic scheduling tool bolted on. Winning for us looks like being the obvious choice for a coordinator who's sick of spending her day on a rota. We talk about capabilities a lot too — support, compliance, the model work Dan's been doing. It's less a fixed plan than something we keep revisiting as customers tell us what actually matters to them.

I don't think we've ever written this out as five separate answers, so I'd be making some of it up if I tried to give you a clean version now. We know roughly who we're selling to and roughly what they buy us for, but the "how we win" and the capabilities piece shift depending on who in the founding four you ask — Marek would probably answer differently to me. It's been an ongoing argument rather than a settled position, and nobody's actually forced the four of us to write it down properly yet.

Ellie's been framing it as an option — switching the model on by default rather than opt-in. For that to work you'd need it actually beating a coordinator on a real rota, not just ours saying so, and right now only four of the eleven have it on so the sample's tiny. Marek reckoned it'd need something like six weeks of a customer running it before you'd trust the output, though that number came from a conversation, not anything written down. Mostly it depends on trust holding through a bad week without someone switching it straight back off.

That's really Priya and Ellie's conversation more than mine — I build what they decide on. In general terms, whatever option we pick has to keep the eleven agencies we've got happy, not just win new logos, because word travels fast in this market. Priya mentioned back in the autumn that renewals mattered more than any new pitch, and I think that's the test underneath most of these choices. My part comes after the decision's made, so I mostly hear the reasoning secondhand rather than sitting in the room where it gets argued out.

I'm honestly not sure which option this is pointing at — that structuring work happens with Ellie and Priya, and I only see it once it's turned into something for me to build. So I can't say what conditions they've set for it to work; I've not been in those sessions and nobody's written the assumptions down anywhere I've seen. If you asked me about the engineering side of a decision I'd have an answer, but the framing itself isn't something I've had reason to look into yet.

If it goes wrong, it's compliance. We push the model into more rotas, onboarding still isn't owned by anyone properly, and a new agency goes live before their carer records are actually clean. Six months later an inspector asks for training history and something's missing or wrong. That agency drops us, and I think Priya reckoned two more would follow within a quarter, though that number came out of a conversation rather than anything we've modelled properly. It's the same crack we already have, just wider, because nobody's picking up the gap between me and Dan on new accounts.

The way this usually breaks for us is onboarding backing up and support drowning. If we take on agencies faster without anyone owning that handoff, tickets pile up and the compliance checks are the first thing that slips because they're already the flakiest part. It's not one clean disaster, it's just everything getting slower until an agency notices and gets annoyed. Dan flagged something similar back in the spring when we added two agencies in the same month and support couldn't keep up. That's probably the shape it takes again, just bigger.

I haven't actually built that story out. We've never sat as a group and mapped what a year of this going wrong would look like — it's always been more reactive, dealing with today's ticket rather than gaming out the whole year. I could guess at pieces, onboarding gaps, compliance breaking under more load, but I'd be assembling that on the spot rather than describing something we've thought through. It's on nobody's list to write yet, and I'm not sure who'd even own pulling it together.

Today it's mostly CareLineLive, or before that, spreadsheets and a whiteboard in the office — Marek reckons about half our eleven came off pure Excel. The main shortcoming is that building next week's rota still eats most of a coordinator's day, and compliance is bolted on rather than built in, so when an inspector asks for three years of training records, someone's digging through folders. I think CareLineLive handles the rota bit okay but the compliance side is thin, though I'd want Priya to confirm that from the sales calls — she hears it more than I do.

Mostly it's manual — agencies patching together spreadsheets, paper compliance folders, sometimes an older system that was built for something bigger than they need. The shortcomings are the obvious ones: it's slow, it's error-prone, and nothing talks to anything else, so a coordinator ends up doing the same check twice. Dan looked into a couple of the bigger incumbents back in January and came away thinking they solve rota but not compliance, or the other way round. It's less that people love what they've got, more that switching feels risky when your business is regulated this tightly.

Honestly I have opinions but not much evidence here. I know the incumbents exist and agencies complain about them, but we've never done a proper comparison — nobody's gone through and mapped what CareLineLive or a plain spreadsheet setup actually fails at against what our customers tell us afterwards. It's tangled up with why people leave a system too, which we haven't tracked properly either. Until someone follows a coordinator through a whole rota cycle on their old tool, I'm working off things people have said to me in passing rather than anything I'd stand behind.

Why - because coordinators were losing most of a day each week just building the rota, that's the number we always quote, though I think it was Dan who first timed it precisely. Who - the coordinator herself, not the registered manager, she's the one under the Friday deadline. How - by cutting that day down to something closer to an hour, though the exact figure moves around depending who you ask and which agency. What - the rota tool and the compliance check underneath it, that's really the two things we sell as one.

That's more or less the shape of every sales conversation I have, though I don't map it out formally like that. I start with why they're on the call, then who's actually going to use it day to day, then what changes for them once it's in. Marek and I talked about writing this up properly as a script back in the spring, but it's stayed just the way I talk, not something we've actually documented or tested against real calls.

I don't think we've ever laid it out in that order as a company - why, who, how, what - as a formal exercise. That's closer to Ellie's territory, she thinks about product that way; I come at things from the sales side, which is messier and more reactive. If someone asked me to give our actual answer to each of those four in sequence, I couldn't do it cleanly right now - I'd need to work through it properly with Ellie rather than improvise it here.

It lands on the coordinator, every week, without fail — that's who's building the rota by hand if we're not there. Before us it was most of a day gone, so multiply that across fifty-two weeks and you're looking at, I don't know, six or seven working weeks a year just lost to a spreadsheet. The sharper cost is the compliance side — an inspector asks for three years of training records and if an agency can't produce them cleanly, that's a failed inspection, and for a forty-carer outfit that's not a fine, that's the business.

It's the thing that keeps agencies up at night, honestly — rotas and compliance both. Coordinators feel it, owners feel it when CQC comes round, carers feel it if a shift's wrong. Marek was talking about this back in the spring, how much anxiety just sits around the paperwork side even when nothing's actually gone wrong yet. Nobody solving it means the whole sector keeps running on people's goodwill and long evenings, which isn't sustainable for a coordinator doing it manually forever. It's a real drag on the industry, not just an inconvenience.

The honest answer is I can't put a figure on the downstream cost — like how often an unresolved rota or compliance gap actually turns into a failed inspection versus just a stressful week. We see the eleven agencies we have, but we've never tracked what happens at agencies still doing it by hand, or what a near-miss costs them. It's not a data set that exists anywhere, and nobody here has gone looking for it — we've been heads-down on our own customers rather than the counterfactual.

That's really more Ellie's territory than mine — product sits with her. But if I think about the compliance checking piece, since that's half of what I do, I'd say yes, there's probably two or three ways in: we could keep pushing the automated flagging we've built, or we could go simpler and just tighten the checklist templates coordinators use by hand. Ellie and Priya were going back and forth on this in a call a few weeks back, I want to say March, and I don't remember which way it landed. So take my read with a pinch of salt.

This one really sits with Ellie rather than me — she's the one who thinks in terms of opportunities and solutions like that, and Priya's close to it too from the sales side. I know there's been some back-and-forth about whether the compliance piece needs more automation or just cleaner templates, sometime around the spring I think, but I wasn't really part of those conversations. My days are mostly onboarding calls and chasing down training records, so I couldn't say with any confidence how many different ways they're actually weighing up.

I don't have a good answer to this one — that kind of framing, opportunity versus solution, isn't something we've actually applied to what we're doing. Ellie might carry it that way in her head, but nobody's written down the different options for the compliance problem and lined them up against each other. It would take someone sitting with coordinators to map out what else could solve the same pain, and that hasn't happened yet, mostly because the rest of us are still just fixing whatever's broken that week.

So when an agency asks for something like a bulk-export button for training records, I'll ask them why — and it almost always comes back to CQC, an inspection's coming and they want three years of records out fast. That's happened maybe three times this year, though the exact count I'd need to check properly before quoting it. One agency, up near Leeds — Sandra, I think her name was — had a bad inspection before us and just never wants to be caught out again. So the thing they ask for is rarely the actual need sitting underneath it.

Usually when a customer asks for a feature I try to get underneath it before we commit engineering time to it. It's become part of how we scope work with agencies — asking why they want something rather than building it as specified, straight off. Dan and Marek find it useful too when they're fielding support requests, because it stops us building the wrong thing for the wrong reason. It's saved us from going down a few blind alleys over the months, more than I'd like to admit really.

I don't have a clean answer to that one, actually — we don't run this consistently across every request that comes in. Sometimes I push on why, sometimes I just take the ask at face value and hand it to Dan or Ellie to weigh up. There's no process behind it yet, it's more instinct depending how the call's going. I'd need to actually track which requests got that follow-up and which didn't before I could tell you whether it changes what we end up building.

That's really Ellie's map more than mine, but the way she's put it to us, the whole thing rests on coordinators trusting the model's rota suggestions enough to actually use them instead of just rebuilding by hand. Riskiest bit, she reckons, is whether it holds up against a busy coordinator on a bad day — four of eleven have turned it on so far, and none of us have properly compared its picks against what a good coordinator would build. I think that's the one that could unravel the whole pitch.

Honestly, for something like Ashvale to keep working, the compliance side has to hold up under an inspection, and coordinators have to trust whatever we hand them enough to act on it without double-checking everything by hand. Priya and Ellie talk about this a lot in terms of what agencies actually bought us for versus what they use day to day. I'd say the riskiest assumption is somewhere in that gap between what we sold and what gets used, but I'm not the one who tracks it closely — that's more their conversation than mine.

I couldn't give you a clean list of assumptions for this one — that's Ellie's territory, and I don't think we've ever written the whole set down in one place, let alone ranked them. What I know is we're leaning on the model behind rota suggestions being one of the newer, shakier assumptions, since only four agencies have it switched on and we haven't checked its output against a coordinator's properly. But which single assumption is riskiest, honestly, is a judgement call nobody's made out loud yet, as far as I've seen.

Last time compliance checking broke — training records mismatch for one of our agencies, back in maybe January — I ended up in a WhatsApp thread with Dan going back and forth on it. There's a spreadsheet somewhere too, one of us patched together the missing dates by hand for the inspector. I don't have the tab open in front of me right now, but I think it lives in the shared drive under compliance fixes. Priya wasn't involved that time, it was just Dan and me firefighting it.

When compliance checking goes wrong we usually just work through it as it comes up, checking the training records against what the agency's got on file. It's usually me or Dan who ends up looking at it, and sometimes Ellie if there's a product angle to it. There isn't really one particular file or thread we go back to for this, it depends on the agency and what's missing that week. We generally just sort it as it comes rather than write it up afterwards, so there's nothing tidy I could point you to.

I couldn't point you to a specific file for this, because we don't keep one. When something breaks with compliance checking it usually gets sorted in whatever channel it comes up in — Slack, a call with the agency, sometimes both — and it doesn't get written up afterwards. That's a decision Priya and Dan would need to weigh in on, whether we start logging these properly. Nobody's made a call on it yet, so there isn't a thread I could pull up and I'd be guessing if I said otherwise.

There's one afternoon that sticks — must've been fourteen, fifteen months in, one of our early agencies rang about an inspection and their coordinator couldn't pull a carer's training record fast enough, the spreadsheet just fell over. That's the day it landed for me that 'compliance checking' wasn't a feature, it was the whole reason they'd bought us. I think it was March, though it might've been April — Marek took that call, not me, so I'm going on what he told me afterwards rather than being in the room.

For me it wasn't one morning, it was watching the pattern build up over a stretch of calls — agencies kept describing the same headache around inspections and rota juggling, and it became obvious our founding assumption was too narrow. Priya was the one fielding most of those conversations, and by early last year she was flagging it in nearly every catch-up. So the realisation was more of a slow tip than a single day, born out of hearing the same complaint often enough that we stopped treating it as an edge case.

I don't have a single day I can point to, and I've stopped trying to force one — the real shift for us was gradual, stitched together from separate conversations, and I never went back to timestamp which one actually flipped it. It's tangled up with Priya's calls, Marek's support tickets, things Dan noticed in usage logs — nobody's pulled that timeline into one place, so the honest answer is I can't isolate the moment, only that by a certain point we all agreed something had changed.

All four show up, but push is the one I hear loudest on calls — it's the coordinator losing most of a day to the rota, every time. Pull is easy, that's our pitch: cut that day down. Anxiety's real too, mostly about handing over three years of training records for an inspection, that's what stalls a signature. Habit is CareLineLive, or just paper if they're smaller. There was a call — February, I think — where a prospect said almost exactly that to me, though I'd have to check who it was before naming her.

It varies call to call, honestly. Some agencies come in already fed up, others get pushed by an inspection going badly, others just like the demo. Marek mentioned a few onboarding conversations back in the autumn that sounded like all four forces at once — the prospect worried and excited in the same breath. Mostly the sales conversation ends up touching everything before contract, so I don't think about it as one force winning over another. It's more that something tips the balance, and it's rarely the same something twice.

I couldn't map that properly for you. I use the four forces loosely in my head on calls, but I've never gone back and coded an actual deal against push, pull, anxiety and habit — that would mean pulling call notes or transcripts, and we don't keep those consistently across all eleven customers. So I've got a feel for it, not an answer. It's the kind of thing I'd want to sit down with Ellie on, since she hears the product side of these conversations too.

The feature I'd pick is compliance checking — if it just worked, coordinators would be thrilled, because that's the bit they actually bought us for, not the rota builder. If we pulled it out tomorrow, I think two or three of the eleven would be genuinely angry, maybe more. That "two or three" is a guess though — I'm reading it off things people have said on support calls with Marek, not off anything we've asked directly. We've never actually sat customers down and asked both halves of that question properly, feature by feature. It's mostly inference from complaints.

With any feature we ship, the reaction splits — some agencies barely notice, others build their whole pitch to their own board around it. Compliance work tends to sit in the second camp, rota suggestions more in the first, at least so far. We generally find out how people feel by what they complain about when it's missing rather than by asking outright. It's useful information, just not tidy, and it comes in through Marek and Priya's calls rather than anything structured. So the honest picture is a rough sense of strong feeling versus mild feeling, not a clean answer per feature.

I can't answer that properly because we've never run the two-sided version of this question on anyone — we ask "what do you like" and "what's missing," but not "how would you feel if this went away," which is a different thing entirely. It's been on my list since roughly the autumn and kept losing to actual bugs. Until I put both halves of that question to a handful of agencies directly, I'd just be inventing their reaction from what I already believe, which isn't the same as knowing it.

This is really more Priya's question than mine—she's the one who talks to agencies about why they buy now rather than five years ago. From what I pick up in onboarding calls, it's something like: CQC got stricter on training-record evidence a few years back, and the older systems weren't built for that kind of scrutiny. Dan mentioned once that CareLineLive's core dates back well over a decade, though I wouldn't swear to that number. That's my best guess, not really my area to be certain about.

That one sits outside my patch—I'm mostly onboarding and compliance checks once an agency's already signed up. Ellie spent some time last spring looking at why the market hadn't moved before us, but I wasn't part of those conversations. What I notice from the coordinator side is people are relieved to have something that isn't a spreadsheet anymore, but the actual reason it took this long isn't something I've got a handle on. Priya would give you a proper answer on this one, not me.

I genuinely have no view on this—it's not a question I've ever had to answer, since my job starts once someone's already decided to buy. Why the market sat unbuilt for years, whether it's regulation, cost of building the software, or agencies being slow to trust cloud tools, that's a Priya and Ellie conversation, not mine. I've never sat in on a pitch where that gets discussed, so I wouldn't know where to start guessing.

The user's the coordinator, not the carer — she's the one under pressure every Sunday night building next week's rota. Her need is speed plus being able to hand an inspector three years of training records without panicking. Capabilities: rota building, which I'd call commodity now, everyone including CareLineLive has a version; compliance checking, which is still bespoke and breaks constantly, though it's what they tell us they bought; and the rota-suggestion model, which is early-stage, four of eleven have switched it on. Dan would probably place compliance further along than I would — we've never actually agreed on that one.

We talk about this a lot in commercial, more than people realise — trying to work out whether an agency's buying us for the coordinator's Sunday-night rota panic or for what happens when CQC comes knocking. Marek and Ellie ran a version of this back in October, mapping what feels settled against what's still held together with workarounds. I lean on that thinking when I'm pricing, because different agencies weight the pieces differently depending on their last inspection. I wouldn't hand you a tidy list of every capability and where each one sits today though — it shifts every time we ship, and nobody's written the current version down.

I don't have an actual answer to that, in the sense of something we've put on paper. We talk in commercial terms — what agencies ask for, what they complain about — not in this language, and none of us has properly laid the four capabilities out against each other and argued where each sits from novel through to commodity. Dan's raised doing something like that a couple of times and it's kept sliding off the list because nothing was on fire. So what I've got is a lived sense of it from calls, not a map I could show you or defend under questioning.

Priya's closer to this than me, but she'll tell you the inertia sits with the agencies still on CareLineLive — coordinators who know its shortcuts and don't want to relearn a system, even a faster one. She mentioned one deal that dragged something like five or six weeks longer than usual because of that, though I'm fuzzy on which account it was. On our side, I'd say the inertia is around compliance checking — Marek's reluctant to rebuild it properly because it's the thing customers say they bought, so nobody wants to be the one who breaks it further.

Inertia's everywhere once you look for it — customers comfortable with what they already know, and us being cautious about changing anything that's working. Marek mentioned something about it back in February, when we were talking about compliance checking, how agencies get used to how it flags things and push back if we change the logic. I think that's the real shape of it, more than any one person or team dragging their feet. It's just the natural pull of things that already work, on both sides of the relationship.

I haven't really worked out where that lands, to be honest — it's not something I've mapped for our own team, and I don't think anyone has written down whose resistance it actually is versus who's just busy. It'd probably need someone going through the sales notes and the support tickets side by side to see where the same objection keeps recurring, and nobody has made that comparison yet as far as I know.

Home care agencies running forty to maybe a hundred and fifty carers — that's roughly our current spread, so yes, I'd say the niche is big enough, there's thousands of agencies that size across the UK. Whether we can lead it, we're ahead of CareLineLive on compliance at least, that's what customers tell us. Adjacent — Priya's talked about domiciliary groups that also run supported living, she reckons that's the natural next step, but I've only caught that in passing, I'd want someone closer to sales to put a proper shape on it before I'd repeat it as settled.

That's really Priya and Ellie's call, not something I've been part of shaping. What I notice from onboarding is that every agency we bring on has basically the same compliance headaches — training records, DBS checks, the same panic before an inspection. That repetition feels like it means something, like there's a proper niche there rather than us just picking up whoever answers the phone. Whether it's big enough on paper, or what comes after it, isn't something anyone's walked me through. I just see the pattern from the inside, agency after agency, and it looks consistent to me.

This is above what I get pulled into. I know we're eleven agencies deep in home care and that's where all my time goes, but whether that's "big enough," or where we go next, is a conversation I've only caught the edges of — Priya and Ellie will have a view, I don't sit in those planning talks. Nobody's shown me numbers on total addressable agencies or mapped an adjacent sector against ours, so I can't say if supported living or something else would be the obvious next step. That's genuinely not decided anywhere I've seen.

We're deliberately not building for the big providers — the enterprise tier sits above us and we've turned away two agencies over two hundred carers who wanted in anyway. That's mostly annoyed Priya, since she's the one saying no on the call while watching revenue walk off. We're also skipping care homes entirely, just domiciliary. I think there were three or four enquiries like that last year — Priya would have the exact count, not me.

There's a whole category of stuff we've quietly parked — payroll integration, care homes rather than home visits, anything that pulls us toward being a bigger platform than four people can run. Marek raised it again this spring, said support kept getting pulled into requests miles outside what we actually sell. We just don't have the hands, so we say no and move on. Priya feels it most, sitting on the calls where it comes up, but I couldn't point you to a specific deal we lost over it.

This one we've never written down properly. We know roughly what we're not doing — payroll, care homes, enterprise — but nobody's gone through and matched that against who it actually annoys, agency by agency. It's more a feeling from calls Priya mentions afterwards than anything tracked. What we'd need is a log of the enquiries we turn away, not just the ones that stuck in someone's memory, and we haven't built that yet, so I'd be guessing if I gave you a name.

If we actually win this segment — become the name coordinators say instead of CareLineLive — what that buys us is trust we can't purchase outright: word of mouth between agencies, and CQC inspectors starting to recognise our exports as credible evidence rather than something to double-check. Dan reckons once we're past maybe twenty-five or thirty agencies that referral loop starts running itself, though that's his gut feel more than anything we've actually measured. We're already seeing early signs with four of the eleven who switched on the model — they talk to each other about it. That reputation is the one thing no marketing spend gets you quickly.

It's the trust piece, mostly. Winning genuinely well in home care means agencies start recommending us to each other, and coordinators trust a system that's been vouched for by someone doing their actual job — that's not something you can just buy with ad spend. Ellie's been talking about this a lot lately, the idea that reputation in this market moves through word of mouth between coordinators rather than through anything we control. It's part of why we've leaned into references and case studies rather than pushing harder on marketing. I think that's the real prize, even if it's hard to put a precise figure on it right now.

That's honestly not something I've worked through properly — my head's usually on the next renewal or the next call, not on what winning the category would unlock years out. We've never compared what it would cost to buy that kind of trust through marketing against just earning it agency by agency. It's the sort of question that needs the four of us in a room together, and as far as I know that conversation hasn't properly happened yet.

This one's not a quick fix, I reckon — it's the compliance checking again. We've patched it three separate times without ever touching how training records actually get stored, so at some point patching stops being honest. I'd call it a full cycle, maybe six weeks if Dan scopes it tight, though he'd probably push back on that number. There was an export that broke for two agencies right before an inspection back in the autumn — that's roughly when I stopped believing another patch would hold.

Depends entirely which bit you mean. Some things landing on my desk are genuinely small — a label change, a checkbox somebody's been asking for — and we just ship those without a conversation. Other things touch nearly everything Dan's built underneath, so calling them quick fixes would be dishonest. Marek raised something back in March that started as a small ask and turned into a much bigger rethink once we actually opened it up and looked at what was underneath it. It's rarely obvious at the start which kind you're dealing with.

I haven't actually settled that for the rota suggestions work. Four agencies have it switched on and I don't yet have a real sense of when the model's wrong versus when a coordinator would've caught it — so I can't tell you whether fixing that gap means a small pass on the model or redesigning how suggestions sit in the rota screen entirely. It depends on what the disagreements actually look like once we compare them properly, and that comparison hasn't happened. Until it does, I'd be guessing rather than shaping anything.

Honestly this is really Dan and Ellie's territory, not mine — but from what I see on the support side, it sits inside the weekly rota screen, there's a toggle in the agency's settings that switches the suggestion layer on. You get to it by building the rota as normal and it just proposes slots instead of you dragging carers in. Four agencies have it on. Where it takes you after that I'm honestly vague on — something about matching training records to shift requirements, but ask Dan, he'll have the actual flow in his head.

That's really a product question — Ellie's the one who'd walk you through where it sits and how someone gets to it. What I can tell you is which agencies have switched it on and that support calls about it come to me and Dan between us, because nobody else picks up that queue. Whether it's one screen or several, whether it hooks into compliance checking directly, I'd be guessing. My side of it is mostly fielding the "why did it suggest that carer" calls once it's already live for someone.

I don't know the answer to this one properly. I've never looked at how the suggestion feature actually threads through the system — I see it from the support queue end, after something's already gone wrong for an agency, not from the architecture side. Dan and Ellie built it and would know where it sits and what it touches. Nobody's walked me through the interactions, so I'd just be inventing a path if I tried to describe it, and I'd rather say that than make something up that sounds tidy.

The one we haven't nailed down is pricing on the rota-suggestion model. It's off by default, and four of the eleven have switched it on. In calls I get asked whether that sits inside the £340 or becomes a new line, and right now I answer differently depending who's asking, which isn't sustainable. Dan and Ellie own the build, but the commercial call is mine — I think we need to settle it before the next renewal wave, sometime around spring, though I'd have to line that up against the actual contract dates before I say it for certain.

Whenever we build something new, the real risk is always on the customer side — will they trust it, will they actually use it day to day. That's been true with the model behind rota suggestions too. Marek picked up a bit of feedback on it back in February, mostly agencies asking how it decides what it decides. I think as long as we're upfront about how it works and don't oversell it, most of that risk settles itself. It's more about managing expectations in the sales conversation than a technical thing we need to lock down in advance.

That's still open on our side — it keeps getting pushed to the end of founder meetings and dropped. I know it touches the model behind rota suggestions, since that's the newest thing we've shipped, but whether the hard call is a technical one for Dan and Ellie to fix, or a pricing one that's mine, hasn't been separated out yet. Nobody's forced that split. Until someone does, I don't have a clean way to answer which assumption we're most exposed on, and I'd rather say that plainly than guess at something we haven't actually decided.

Ellie runs that conversation, not me — I just hear the outcome. This cycle it was: no bespoke integrations for a single agency, and nobody touches the core compliance logic while the model's still being tested on those four accounts. I think she also ruled out anything that pulls Marek off onboarding, since that's already stretched thin. She pinned it in our shared doc sometime in the last month or so, though I couldn't give you the exact date.

There's a general list Ellie keeps each cycle — things we agree not to touch so the actual bets get finished. It covers stuff like big integration requests, one-off customer asks, anything that turns into scope creep. Priya's usually the one pushing back on customers when something falls outside it, and Marek flags it if a support ticket starts drifting that way. It's more a discipline thing than a fixed rulebook — the point is nobody quietly expands a bet mid-cycle.
